Campus mess kitchens decide how much food to cook before they know how many students
will eat, and the gap between the two ends up as avoidable waste. PrePlate is a full-stack web
application that closes this information gap. Students log in with their registration number,
view the day’s breakfast, lunch, snacks and dinner menus with calorie and nutrient details, and
confirm whether they will attend before a meal-specific deadline; they can also select the dishes
they plan to eat into a My Plate summary, review their food history and see personal analytics.
A server-side scheduler reminds students who have not responded thirty minutes before each
deadline. Kitchen administrators manage dishes and menus, watch live response counts,
receive an attendance forecast with a recommended preparation quantity for every dish, and
record what was actually consumed so that waste can be analysed. The system comprises a
React single page application, a Spring Boot backend with a MySQL database, and a separate
FastAPI forecasting service. The service uses linear regression chosen by validation error, 90
percent prediction intervals and a five percent safety buffer; when it is unavailable or history
is insufficient, the backend returns a clearly labelled heuristic forecast. On a synthetic
evaluation dataset of 1,680 meals, the selected models reduced mean absolute error by 56.5
percent for attendance and 42.9 percent for dish quantity compared with the statistical fallback.
The project was delivered in three equal sprints (AI service, frontend, backend and integration)
over about one month by a two-member team and deployed on free cloud tiers, supporting UN
Sustainable Development Goal 12 on responsible consumption.

PrePlate is a full-stack web application that connects the students who eat in a campus mess
with the kitchen that feeds them. A kitchen can cook the right amount of food only if it knows,
ahead of time, how many people will eat and which dishes they are likely to take. PrePlate
collects this information from students in a lightweight way, turns it into a demand forecast
with a recommended preparation quantity for every dish, and then measures what was actually
consumed so that both the forecast and the kitchen’s practice improve over time.
The application serves two kinds of users. Students log in with their registration number, see
the breakfast, lunch, snacks and dinner menus with nutritional information, confirm whether
they will attend each meal before its deadline, select the dishes they intend to eat into a “My
Plate” summary, receive reminders and review their own food history. Kitchen administrators
manage dishes and menus, watch live response counts, receive an AI-generated attendance
forecast and recommended quantity per dish, and record prepared and consumed quantities to
analyse waste. Technically, PrePlate consists of a React single page application, a Spring Boot

Food waste is a large and measurable problem. The UNEP Food Waste Index Report 2024
estimates that about 1.05 billion tonnes of food was wasted worldwide in 2022, roughly one
fifth of the food available to consumers [1]. Institutional kitchens such as university messes are
a good place to act because they cook in large batches for a predictable population and make
preparation decisions on a fixed daily schedule.
In a typical campus mess the quantity to cook is decided from habit and from the previous
day’s experience. Students are not asked in advance whether they will eat, so the kitchen cannot
tell a normal day from a day on which many students are away. The usual outcome is a safe
over-estimate, paid for in wasted food, money and effort, with the occasional shortage at the
end of the serving window. Both outcomes have the same cause: the kitchen and the students
have no channel for exchanging information before cooking begins. PrePlate builds that
channel so that responding takes only a few seconds, gives something back to the student, and
gives the kitchen a number it can act on.

1.4 Sustainable Development Goal of the Project
PrePlate contributes primarily to UN Sustainable Development Goal 12, Responsible
Consumption and Production, and in particular to Target 12.3, which aims to halve per-capita
food waste at the retail and consumer levels and to reduce food losses along supply chains by
2030 [2]. By giving the kitchen advance knowledge of demand and a recommended quantity
for each dish, PrePlate attacks over-preparation at its source, the decision about how much to
cook, rather than managing leftovers afterwards. The waste analytics module makes the result
visible, which is a prerequisite for improvement.
The project also supports SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), because food that is not wasted remains
available to people, and SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), because the application shows
calories, protein, carbohydrates and fat for every dish and for the student’s planned plate. The
“food for thought” facts on the student home page build awareness of sustainable eating.
For students and kitchen staff of a campus mess who waste food because the kitchen cannot
see demand, PrePlate is a meal-attendance and demand-forecasting web application that lets
students respond to meals in seconds and tells the kitchen how much to prepare. Unlike a plain
notice board or a manual headcount, PrePlate combines deadline-aware responses with a
machine-learning forecast and closes the loop with measured waste.
Primary: students who eat in the campus mess. Secondary: mess managers, kitchen
administrators and college administration interested in sustainability metrics.

The forecasting service is a separate FastAPI application because the machine learning stack
(Python, scikit-learn, XGBoost) differs from the Java backend and has its own release cycle; a
separate process also lets the model fail without taking the application down. Its offline pipeline
generates data, splits it by date, trains three candidate models for each target, selects the best
by validation error, calibrates an interval on a separate period and stores a versioned bundle.
The online part loads the bundle and serves requests (figure 2.1). Training and serving share
the same feature code, which prevents training/serving skew.
Figure 2.1 Offline pipeline and online serving of the forecasting service
The synthetic dataset covers 420 consecutive days (1,680 meal records and 7,117 dish records)
and is split by date into 252 days for training, 63 for validation, 42 for interval calibration and
63 for the final test, so that no row of a date is shared between parts. The attendance model
uses the eligible students, the yes / unsure / no-response rates, the historical attendance rate and
waste percentage, the number of dishes, the average menu interest and popularity, and one-hot
indicators for meal type and weekday. The dish model adds the dish’s own student interest,
historical popularity and average consumed quantity.
The backend and the service exchange JSON over HTTPS in real time, one request per meal.
The service validates every request strictly: the response counts must sum to the number of
eligible students, no dish interest may exceed the eligible students, and dish identifiers must be
unique. Table 2.4 shows the fields of POST /forecast/details.

Kitchens in campus messes cook without advance knowledge of attendance or
dish preference, resulting in avoidable food waste and occasional shortage.
A web system collects per-meal attendance responses and dish preferences under
meal-specific deadlines, generates time-based reminders relative to the server
clock, and sends aggregated responses with historical consumption to a
forecasting service. The service returns predicted attendance and per-dish
quantities with a prediction interval and a safety-buffered recommended quantity;
the backend falls back to a labelled heuristic when the service is unavailable or
history is insufficient. Recorded consumption closes the loop for waste analytics

Demand and attendance forecasting for catering is established: machine-learning
models for campus dining demand [14], guest attendance in school canteens [15],

school [17]. US 2005/0154560 A1 [18] covers real-time prediction of restaurant

reviewed collects student-declared attendance and dish intent under per-meal
deadlines, issues deadline-relative reminders, and returns a source-labelled
forecast with a prediction interval, safety buffer and automatic fallback. This was

Kitchens in campus messes cook without advance knowledge of attendance or  dish preference, resulting in avoidable food waste and occasional shortage.

A web system collects per-meal attendance responses and dish preferences under  meal-specific deadlines, generates time-based reminders relative to the server  clock, and sends aggregated responses with historical consumption to a  forecasting service.
